outcomes: Data-driven targeting led to investments in green and cool infrastructure across the city’s heat-prone zones; Thousands of trees, cool roofs, and green roofs were installed—green roofs now feature on City Hall and commercial buildings; Heat-resilient planning was institutionalized in Chicago’s 2008 Climate Action Plan and Cook County’s Hazard Mitigation strategy; Increased community awareness and capacity to respond to heat emergencies, especially in at-risk neighborhoods.

summary: In Chicago, IL, Chicago Uses Green Infrastructure to Reduce Extreme Heat is a monitoring and adaptive management initiative. The program uses climate vulnerability assessment and introduced green roofs, cool roofs (EPA Energy Star standards), and expanded tree canopy via incentives like expedited permits and tax-funded grants. The case addresses extreme Heat, Flooding. title: Chicago Uses Green Infrastructure to Reduce Extreme Heat
transferability: Seattle and other urban centers in Washington face similar challenges related to urban heat islands and the disproportionate impacts on vulnerable populations. By adopting Chicago’s more robust approach—which includes heat risk mapping, widespread deployment of green infrastructure, integration of adaptation into building codes, and a strong focus on equitable outreach—Washington cities can strengthen public health, advance climate justice, and build community resilience to extreme heat. Unlike Chicago, much of Seattle’s current building code incentives are voluntary, highlighting an opportunity to shift toward more comprehensive and enforceable strategies.
